The species Mucropetraliella stemmatum was described by Maria Susan Sanjay, C. Venkatraman, S. Shrinivaasu 
and Soja Louis based on a Holotype and a Paratype collected from Manalli putti Island at 4m depth (9°12’50.5”N 
79°07’53.7”E) in the Gulf of Mannar Marine Biosphere Reserve on the East coast of India, India. The type 
specimen has been deposited in ZSI-MBRC. The species is named due to arrangement of the avicularia in a ring 
like fashion around the orifice like a garland around the neck.

The Chilopoda are a group of predatory arthropods more commonly known as centipedes 
are major components of soil biodiversity distributed throughout the temperate and 
tropical regions of the world. They are economically important group of arthropods which 
play valuable roles in the terrestrial ecosystems helping to control noxious insect pests. 
They are often treated as creatures of nuisance owing to their poisonous and painful 
bite, particularly of the members of the family Scolopendridae.  Centipedes inhabit wet, 
moist places and the environs below rotten barks, dry foliage, stones and also in cow 
dung heap. They are soft-bodied and dorsoventrally flattened having one pair of legs in 
each trunk segment. The number of body segments vary from 15-200 and body size 1 to 
30cm. The class Chilopoda is divided into five orders; Geophilomorpha (soil centipedes), 
Lithobiomorpha (rock or garden centipedes), Scolopendromorpha (tropical or giant 
centipedes), Scutigeromorpha (house or feather centipedes) and Craterostigmomorpha. 
Among the four orders of Chilopoda known from India (Scolopendromoprha, 
Lithobiomorpha, Scutigeromorpha and Geophilomorpha), major studies are undertaken 
only on Scolopendromorpha. . This year only one new species of Chilopoda has been 
described from Karnataka.

The Dipteran fauna commonly referred to as flies is a category of insects characterized 
by two wings and two halteres. Their vast array of ecosystem services, origins, and 
distributional variations have collectively rendered these dipteran flies a vital component 
of any global ecosystem. The group’s economic significance is substantial, as they serve 
as predators and parasitoids of other insects, aid in pest management, and contribute to 
nutrient cycling, from soil turnover, forensic investigations, and decomposition of biological 
materials to the blooming of plants; this collection of true flies has provided considerable 
economic and aesthetic advantages as well as cultural importance to human society. 
This year a total of 23 species of Diptera have been described from India, West Bengal (6), 
Meghalaya (4), Karnataka (3), Arunachal Pradesh (2), Himachal Pradesh (2), Andhra Pradesh 
(1), Goa (1), Uttarakhand (1), Tamil Nadu (1), Jammu & Kashmir (1) and Andaman & Nicobar 
Islands (1).

The species Asphondylia mangiferi was described 
by Peter Kolesik, K.J. David, D.S. Reddy, B.S. 
Gotyal, and RS Ramya based on a Holotype and 
seven Paratypes collected from Maruvada village 
(17.39131°N, 82.53448°E), Andhra Pradesh, 
India. The type specimen is deposited at ICAR-
NBAIR. The new species is named after the generic 
name of its host plant.
The species Lasioptera sharma was described by 
Duraikannu Vasanthakumar, Rajiv Loganathan, 
and Palanisamy Senthilkumar based on a Holotype 
and several Paratypes collected from Mollem 
(15.3777°N; 74.23059°E), Goa, India. The type 
specimen is deposited at WRC-ZSI. The species is 
named in the honour of Dr. Radheshyam Muralidhar 
Sharma, an eminent Indian Cecidologist.

The species Forcipomyia (Forcipomyia) arcuatilis 
was described by Gouri Sankar Pal, Lipika Ghosh 
and Niladri Hazra based on a Holotype and four 
Paratypes collected from Lepchakha (26.75332°N, 
89.59151°E), Alipurduar, West Bengal, India. 
The type specimen is housed at the Entomological 
Collection of the Department of Zoology, The 
University of Burdwan (India). The specific epithet 
derives from the Latin arcus (= bow) and refers to 
the “bow-shaped” appearance of the fused lateral 
process of the parameres.
